name: Beard balm
lead: Beard balm is a thick grooming product made from butters and beeswax, often with carrier oils, applied to a clean beard to condition it and hold its shape. Users work it through the beard and comb it to tame flyaways, soften coarse hair and give the outline a tidier, more defined shape, so a beard looks fuller and better groomed. [3] It styles the hair that is already there and is not a growth product.

Beeswax, the usual hold ingredient, is also used in moustache wax and hair pomades, which Wikipedia says make hair look sleek and shiny; its main components are esters of fatty acids and long-chain alcohols, and it softens near body temperature, which is why the warmth of the hands spreads the product. [4] Butters such as shea butter, a triglyceride fat rich in stearic and oleic acids, are widely used in cosmetics as emollients and skin conditioners. [7]

Balms became common as beards returned to fashion in the 2010s, a decade in which Wikipedia reports that full beards became fashionable again among young men and sales of male grooming products rose sharply. [1] No clinical research on beard balms was found. The beard itself is studied by evolutionary and dermatology researchers as an androgen-dependent secondary sexual characteristic, with studies on how beards affect perceived age, dominance and attractiveness; that literature concerns facial hair rather than the product. [1][2]

angle.text: Balm is used after washing to control flyaways and set the beard's outline, so the beard looks neater and more intentional through the day. It affects appearance and feel until the next wash.

infobox: Butters (such as shea), beeswax, carrier oils [4][7]
Firmer than beard oil; softens at body temperature [4]

paras: Balms are firmer than beard oils. The wax component is described as forming a light film that holds hairs in place, while butters and oils soften and add moisture; warmth from the hands spreads the product. [4] Users typically scoop a small amount, warm it between the hands and work it through a clean, dry or towel-dried beard, then comb or brush it into shape.

Balms sit between oils, which mainly soften and add sheen, and waxes, which give stronger hold. Moustache wax is related, and Wikipedia lists beeswax among the ingredients of moustache wax, lip balms, hand creams and salves. [4]
Wikipedia describes beeswax as having a melting point of about 62 to 64 C and softening at body temperature, and notes that adulterated beeswax may contain paraffin and other additives. [4]

Shea butter, a common balm base, is a fat made mostly of stearic and oleic acids, about 85 to 90 percent of its fatty acids. Stearic acid makes it firm, and oleic acid determines how soft it is at a given temperature. It comes from the nut of the African shea tree, which grows wild across the West African savannah, and is used in cosmetics as an emollient and skin conditioner. [7] Carrier oils are often added for softness and spreadability.

Grooming the beard with oils and tongs is old: Wikipedia describes Mesopotamian men oiling and dressing their beards and creating ringlets and tiered patterns with tongs and curling irons, Greek men curling beards, and Egyptian rulers dyeing chin hair with henna. [1] Beards declined through the early twentieth century, returned with beatniks in the 1950s and hippies in the mid-1960s, declined again by the early 1980s, and became fashionable among young men in the 2010s. [1] Modern beard balms belong to that last revival and the accompanying growth in men's grooming products. [1]

On T Nation, members mention balm as part of a quick routine for a coarse beard: one poster says combing and rubbing in balm keeps hair that would otherwise become painful from daily tangling manageable, and another gets by with a grocery-store argan oil and no specialty beard oils or balms. [3][5] Another thread describes grooming products from specialty shaving stores as a way to get into a routine. [6]

A training-log poster reports using a tattoo balm as the best beard balm they had tried and plans to test a cheaper brand. [8] These posts reflect personal preferences rather than controlled comparisons; no study compares balms with oils, and members differ on whether premium products matter.

Wikipedia describes the beard as androgen-dependent facial hair whose social meaning has varied across cultures and eras. Evolutionary explanations include signalling sexual maturity and dominance by making the jaw look larger, and the article cites a study in which clean-shaven faces were rated less dominant than bearded ones. [1] Scholars disagree about whether beard-related sexual selection is driven by attractiveness or dominance. [1] Those studies do not test grooming products.
Heavy use can leave residue, weigh down the beard and clog skin if not washed out. Fragrance and nut-based ingredients can irritate or trigger allergy in some people. Effects last until washing.
